trace.raw: {"text": "In the realm of adolescent social network research, the correlation between substance use and friendship formation is well-documented. Non-AI researchers have used the recurring connection between substance use and friendship formation as a basis for intervention research with promising results [47]. Our study’s finding that substance use is not associated with relational patterns among 9th and 10th-grade AI youth marks a significant departure from established trends, offering a novel perspective. This finding not only underscores a fundamental lack of theoretical understanding regarding developmental relationship patterns within this demographic but also signals the urgent need to explore more deeply the factors influencing relational dynamics among AI youth. Because the conventional assumption in much of the adolescent health literature, that risky behavior is a primary determinant of relationships in youth, does not hold in our study, which may also mean that common network intervention strategies aimed at reducing substance use may not be as effective as previously thought [4,5,10]. The prevalent approach to adolescent social network interventions for substance use prevention often hinges on the presumption that friendship ties are, to some extent, founded on substance use behaviors. Given that this assumption does not align with our findings, it becomes imperative to investigate culturally relevant alternatives to understanding of how substance use relates to friendship formation. Gaining insight into these alternative predictors is crucial for developing innovative, effective strategies for substance use prevention tailored to AI youth that may center on strengths-based connections rather than social ties rooted in risky behavior.", "page": 16}

trace.raw: {"text": "The literature highlights the role that school transitions (elementary to middle to high school) play in adolescent networks, but our cross-sectional design imposes a fundamental interpretive limit: a single, simultaneous observation of the network and of individual attributes cannot capture changes in network formation and behavior over time. More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time [4,18,48].", "page": 1}
